**I’d pivot toward a portable edge-agent platform.** The developer promise is compelling: develop an agent on your laptop, deploy it to supported devices, and preserve its tools, permissions, and execution history.

Your horizontal-versus-vertical distinction helps explain the architecture. The product differentiation needs to be more specific, though.

LiteRT-LM already supports cross-platform execution, multimodal input, and function calling—including manually handling tool calls before execution. Google ADK also already provides an agent layer above LiteRT-LM and other model providers. So “an agent runtime above inference runtimes” is an existing category. [LiteRT-LM features](https://github.com/google-ai-edge/LiteRT-LM), [tool execution controls](https://developers.google.com/edge/litert-lm/android), [ADK integration](https://adk.dev/agents/models/litert-lm/)

**The opportunity I see is making deployment across edge hardware predictable.** That includes the difficult parts developers currently have to reconcile: compatible model artifacts, runtime dependencies, available sensors, tool permissions, and evidence of what actually executed.

The pitch I’d use:

> **PHASEONE packages your agent for the edge. One application definition, native execution across supported engines, and consistent permissions wherever it runs.**

I’d give that product four concrete responsibilities:

| Component | What PHASEONE would own |
|---|---|
| **Agent package** | Workflow, prompts, tool schemas, permissions, model variants, dependency versions, and signed artifact digests. |
| **Device resolver** | Detect hardware and runtime capabilities, select a compatible variant, and explain missing requirements before execution. |
| **Tool gateway** | Validate each requested action, enforce permissions, hold scoped credentials, and record the result. |
| **Session and receipts** | Preserve messages and tool results; record the actual model, backend, device, timing, and policy decisions. |

A few boundaries make this credible:

- **Portability belongs to the application contract.** A package can contain separate `.litertlm` and `.pte` variants. Qualcomm exports require target SoC and compiler settings; the sponsor’s QCS8275 artifacts do not establish compatibility with a Mac or another NPU. [ExecuTorch Qualcomm documentation](https://github.com/pytorch/executorch/blob/main/docs/source/backends-qualcomm.md)
- **Session migration should reconstruct context from messages and tool results.** Treat KV caches as engine-specific, and expect different models to produce different answers.
- **Vision, embeddings, and audio should be typed capabilities.** Expose operations such as `embed`, `transcribe`, or `estimate_depth`; give conversational models their own interface.
- **Permissions require control over execution.** The gateway must hold the relevant credentials or sit behind an enforced sandbox boundary. A signature establishes package provenance and integrity; it does not establish that the model’s behavior is safe.

For the hackathon, I’d make the demonstration **one package, two real runtimes, one visible hardware action**:

1. Build a small workbench assistant with tools to read device status and toggle the board’s indicator.
2. Run it through LiteRT-LM on the Mac, then deploy the same application definition through ExecuTorch on the VENTUNO Q. Show which model artifact and backend each run selected.
3. Request an action outside its permissions. Show the gateway rejecting it consistently and recording the reason.
4. Modify a signed package file and demonstrate rejection before loading.

That tells a developer-tooling story while retaining the security work as a useful product feature. The Brio, MCU, and board become capabilities applications can request. The existing PHASEONE Gate becomes the first example application.

Our current code already supplies useful pieces: policy, scoped credentials, MCP, audit records, and hardware adapters. **The new critical milestone is completing the same bounded task through two actual inference engines.** Sponsor QNN execution is still unverified, and the LiteRT-LM integration would be new work; those remain explicit in the [project status](</Users/mac/ventuno-hackathon/hackathon-submission/PHASEONE[tpu]/STATUS.md>).

I’d make that two-engine demonstration the decision point before expanding into a broader “universal” platform.

full:
**The biggest gap is that we haven’t defined what “portable” guarantees.** Loading an agent, getting useful behavior, meeting a latency budget, and preserving permissions are four different promises.

Here’s the weak dismissal, the strongest case against it, and the strongest case for it.

**The strawman:** “It’s just a wrapper around other people’s runtimes.”

That criticism alone is weak. An abstraction can be valuable when it removes substantial integration work. The real question is **how much work disappears for the developer—and how much maintenance we inherit.**

**The strongest case against it:** Developers may already get enough portability from one runtime plus an existing agent framework.

LiteRT-LM already supports several platforms, tools, and multimodal inputs. ADK already supplies sessions and callbacks that can inspect or block tool execution. Foundry Local already handles hardware selection and model lifecycle management. These overlap significantly with our proposed feature list. [LiteRT-LM](https://github.com/google-ai-edge/LiteRT-LM), [ADK callbacks](https://adk.dev/callbacks/), [Foundry Local architecture](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry-local/concepts/foundry-local-architecture)

The skeptical customer’s argument would be:

> “I deploy on one hardware family. Why adopt your framework, debug your adapters, and accept another dependency when my existing stack works?”

That’s a serious objection. Supporting more engines only creates value when customers actually need those engines. Meanwhile, every additional model, quantization, runtime version, and device increases our testing burden.

**The strongest case for it:** Teams shipping agents across different devices repeatedly encounter the same integration problems.

They need a model that fits, a compatible runtime, working sensors, predictable tools, recovery after disconnects, and a way to diagnose failures. If PHASEONE can turn that into a tested deployment package with clear compatibility guarantees, it could save meaningful engineering time.

The valuable promise becomes:

> “Here is your agent, the devices it supports, the behavior we tested, and the evidence that this deployment works.”

That is the version I would pursue.

The main system gaps are:

| Missing piece | Where it breaks | What we would need |
|---|---|---|
| **Artifact build and compatibility pipeline** | A manifest selects a model whose compiled backend, driver requirements, or input shapes don’t match the device. | Reproducible exports, pinned dependencies, a tested compatibility matrix, and actionable preflight checks. |
| **Behavioral compatibility tests** | Both engines accept the request, but one model chooses the wrong tool, loses a constraint, or exhausts its context window. | Tests of task outcomes, tool arguments, refusals, and context limits for every supported model variant. |
| **An enforced execution boundary** | The agent can bypass our gateway and access files, credentials, or devices directly. | Scoped executors, process isolation where necessary, and credentials held behind the gateway. |
| **Crash and reconnect semantics** | The board executes an action, disconnects before acknowledging it, and the host retries it. | Durable action IDs, duplicate detection, acknowledgments, and explicit recovery for uncertain outcomes. |
| **Resource management** | Several models individually fit, but loading them together causes memory pressure, long model swaps, or missed deadlines. | Memory budgets, scheduling, cancellation, warm-up measurements, and explicit fallback policies. |
| **Package and update lifecycle** | A signed model is paired with changed prompts, tokenizer files, tools, or runtime binaries; an update breaks existing devices. | Integrity coverage for the whole application, trusted signing keys, versioned state, and recoverable updates. |

The first row is substantial engineering. ExecuTorch’s Qualcomm path explicitly requires target SoC and compiler configuration; abstraction does not remove that work. It makes us responsible for organizing and validating it. [Qualcomm backend documentation](https://github.com/pytorch/executorch/blob/main/docs/source/backends-qualcomm.md)

A concrete failure worth designing around: **“toggle the LED” is dangerous to retry blindly.** If the first attempt succeeded, the retry reverses it. “Set the LED to on,” combined with a recorded action ID and a state check, gives us a much better recovery story. The same issue becomes consequential with actuators or file changes.

There’s also a product decision still unresolved: **are we hosting the complete agent, providing inference to an existing agent, or exposing portable tools?** Each gives us different control. If we provide inference alone, we cannot guarantee what the surrounding application does with the output. I would choose an application package and device host that can integrate with existing agent frameworks.

For the security claims, our current boundary remains limited. The existing architecture explicitly acknowledges that the Mac can bypass hooks, access host-held credentials, and keep processes running after a screen lock. A separate board gives us separation, but enforcement still depends on which resources it controls. [Current trust boundaries](</Users/mac/ventuno-hackathon/hackathon-submission/PHASEONE[tpu]/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md>)

**My recommendation is to make “verified deployment” the center of the product.** Start with one useful application, two engines, and two targets. Require it to:

- Pass the same task and permission tests on both.
- Report its actual model and accelerator.
- Recover from a disconnect without repeating an action.
- Reject incompatible packages before starting.
- Deploy from a clean setup without application-specific fixes.

We already have useful policy, audit, and hardware integration code. We still need the two-engine application demonstration; sponsor QNN execution remains pending in the [project status](</Users/mac/ventuno-hackathon/hackathon-submission/PHASEONE[tpu]/STATUS.md>).

The business hypothesis to test is whether developers value those guarantees enough to adopt another dependency. The technical hypothesis is whether we can provide them without every new target becoming a bespoke integration project.

**Yes—those can fit into the ecosystem, but they belong at different integration points.** We need to distinguish tools that **prepare models**, engines that **execute models**, and libraries that **provide complete tasks**. I’m reading your list as **MLC LLM, Microsoft’s ONNX Runtime, and Olive**. MLC LLM is a separate project from Microsoft’s stack. | Technology | What it actually provides | Where it fits in PHASEONE | |---|---|---| | **[MLC LLM](https://llm.mlc.ai/)** | Model compilation plus an LLM execution engine across platforms. | A build adapter **and** a runtime adapter. | | **[WebLLM](https://webllm.mlc.ai/)** | Browser LLM inference using the MLC ecosystem and WebGPU. | A browser conversation backend. | | **[ONNX Runtime / ORT GenAI](https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/genai/)** | ONNX is the model format; ONNX Runtime executes models. ORT GenAI adds tokenization, generation, sampling, and KV-cache management. | A tensor backend, plus a conversation backend through GenAI. | | **[Olive](https://microsoft.github.io/Olive/how-to/cli/cli-run.html)** | Conversion, quantization, optimization, evaluation, and packaging workflows. | Our **build pipeline** invokes it to produce deployment artifacts. | | **LiteRT / [LiteRT.js](https://developers.google.com/edge/litert/web/get_started)** | General model execution; LiteRT.js brings that to the browser. | Native and browser inference adapters for typed tasks. | | **LiteRT-LM / [LiteRT-LM Web](https://developers.google.com/edge/litert-lm/js)** | Higher-level language-model execution and conversations. | Native and browser conversation adapters. | | **[MediaPipe Tasks](https://developers.google.com/edge/mediapipe/solutions/guide)** | Packaged capabilities such as detection, landmarks, classification, and embeddings. | Task providers exposed through operations such as `detect_faces` or `embed_text`. | **Olive is the clearest distinction:** it helps produce what we deploy. It generally isn’t the engine receiving each agent inference request. Its documented workflows can output an optimized ONNX model and runtime configuration together. I’d structure our proposed layer like this: ```mermaid flowchart TD B["Build adapters
Olive · MLC compiler · model exporters"] P["Versioned package
Application + target-specific artifacts"] H["PHASEONE host
Capability checks · sessions · policy · audit"] N["Native runtime adapters"] W["Browser runtime adapters"] T["Task providers
MediaPipe · vision · audio"] X["Permission-controlled tool executor"] B --> P P --> H H --> N H --> W H --> T H --> X ``` The important design choice is **separate build adapters from execution adapters**. Otherwise, we end up forcing very different products into an interface that cannot describe them accurately. The Google naming confusion also has a concrete explanation: - **LiteRT.js**, distributed as `@litertjs/core`, runs general `.tflite` models. - **LiteRT-LM Web**, distributed as `@litert-lm/core`, provides the conversation interface for supported `.litertlm` models. - **MediaPipe Tasks** provides higher-level task pipelines. - The older **MediaPipe LLM Inference API is now maintenance-only**, and Google recommends migrating that API to LiteRT-LM. That statement applies to its LLM API, not to all of MediaPipe. [Migration notice](https://developers.google.com/edge/mediapipe/solutions/genai/llm_inference) For the web, we need to distinguish **where inference happens**: | Deployment | Where computation happens | |---|---| | Browser loads WebLLM, LiteRT-LM Web, LiteRT.js, or ORT Web | On the computer running that browser, through its available browser backends. | | Browser calls our VENTUNO service | On the board, using the board’s installed native runtime and accelerator. | A page open on your Mac does not gain access to the VENTUNO’s NPU just by choosing WebGPU or WebNN. The board needs a native service, and the page communicates with it. The board should enforce permissions for its own tools. Browser execution also needs its own compatibility profile. Google currently describes LiteRT.js’s WebNN path as experimental, with platform and configuration requirements. “Supports web” cannot imply “uses an NPU in every browser.” [LiteRT.js requirements](https://developers.google.com/edge/litert/web/get_started) **The package would carry a choice of compatible implementations.** For example, one conversation capability could have an ExecuTorch variant for the board and a LiteRT-LM Web variant for the browser. Both implement the same application-facing contract; each retains its own model files, preprocessing, context limits, and tested capabilities. That does **not** imply automatic conversion between the sponsor’s `.pte`, ONNX, MLC, and `.litertlm` artifacts. Those variants need to be supplied or built and validated. For our hackathon scope, I’d support **ExecuTorch on the VENTUNO plus one browser conversation engine**, and design the interfaces to accommodate the others. MLC already explicitly pursues universal deployment, so our differentiation needs to remain **tested application deployment, consistent tool permissions, and useful failure diagnostics across engines**. Adding more runtime names alone won’t establish that value.

**PHASEONE is a portable runtime for AI applications—one integration for shipping across phones, laptops, browsers, and edge devices.**

Build against PHASEONE, and let the runtime handle compatible model packages, execution backends, and device capabilities. Your application keeps a consistent interface for inference, tools, and sessions as the hardware underneath it changes.

LiteRT, ExecuTorch, ONNX Runtime, and MLC provide powerful model execution engines. PHASEONE builds on those engines, giving developers a common application layer across them. You can use the engine that fits each supported device while keeping your application code and deployment workflow consistent.

Use an underlying engine directly when you want detailed control over its implementation. Choose PHASEONE when your priority is shipping and maintaining one AI product across a changing mix of devices and runtimes—with compatibility, verification, and permission checks built in.

**My honest read: we’ve proved parts of the technology, but haven’t yet proved the runtime earns its complexity.** The problem being real doesn’t automatically make our solution compelling.

LiteRT-LM already provides multiple platforms, conversations, and tools. Our value has to be the integration work developers can stop doing. [Google’s overview](https://developers.google.com/edge/litert-lm/overview).

I’d pitch the intended product as:

> **PHASEONE is a runtime for shipping local AI applications across the devices your customers use—without maintaining a separate AI integration for every stack.**

For Gate, that becomes tangible: **“I built a physical AI referee. I can change its models and deployment hardware while keeping the application.”** Camera processing, operator intent, decision rules, and intervention controls stay together as a product.

The exciting outcome is **getting from an AI prototype to something other people can actually deploy.** Backend switching is one mechanism supporting that.

My recommendation: **keep the runtime as the deliverable, freeze additional platform features, and make Gate prove the benefit.** A second developer should be able to deploy Gate on another supported configuration without becoming an ExecuTorch or LiteRT specialist. If they still need to untangle both stacks themselves, we have more work to do before the pitch holds up.

**Your examples identify what’s missing: PHASEONE must manage shipping and updating compatible model variants—not just expose inference calls.**

The app calls a logical model such as `screen-reader`. PHASEONE owns the implementation selected for that device:

| Situation | PHASEONE’s responsibility |
|---|---|
| Developing on a laptop | Run a compatible desktop variant with the same application contract. |
| Shipping to either phone | Fetch the qualified model, preprocessing, and runtime configuration for that device. |
| A better compatible model appears | Adopt a new model release without rewriting the app’s AI integration. |
| A new native delegate appears | Update the SDK/app module as needed, while preserving the application API. |

That last distinction matters: **new model data and new native code have different update paths.** Play AI Packs themselves update with the app binary. [Google’s delivery documentation](https://developer.android.com/google/play/on-device-ai).

The research also confirms we have infrastructure to reuse: LiteRT already provides multi-vendor NPU selection and targeted delivery, and ExecuTorch already has a MediaTek backend. PHASEONE should coordinate these across runtimes, development machines, and deployed devices. [LiteRT](https://developers.google.com/edge/litert/next/npu), [ExecuTorch](https://docs.pytorch.org/executorch/stable/android-mediatek.html).

- An embedded Android SDK that executes locally on both phones.
- A model-release catalog that downloads only the selected variant.
- Compatibility checks and task-quality validation before activation, with rollback.

The existing API, adapters, packages, and Mac/Linux execution remain the foundation. Further engine families and attestation features can wait.
